title: Serialization format of analyses
text:
Syntactic analyses produce a list of Sentence objects, VerbalExpression objects, and TokenAnalysis objects. These are serialized to a plain-text format with delimited-text data blocks identified by labels for each, identified by the labels #!sentences, #!verbal_units and #!tokens respectively. A fourth, optional block with metatadata about the language model and its reasoning is identified by the label #!lm. Blocks may appear in any order and may repeat (e.g. from concatenating data from multiple analyses).
The delimited-text structure of each block’s data directly translates the structure of the object it is serializing. None fields are serialized as an empty string (""). By default, the pipe character | is used as a delimiter in delimited-text blocks.

title: Serialization format of analyses
text:
Field structure of each block
The structure of each block type is illustrated with the serialization of an analysis of a passage with text content arma virumque cano and CTS URN urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1.

#!sentences
Sentence blocks have four columns with a header context_begin|first_token|context_end|last_token. These give the URN content and token ID of the first and last tokens of each sentence.
Example:
#!sentences
context_begin|first_token|context_end|last_token
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t0|urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t3


#!verbal_units
Verbal unit blocks begin with a header context|token|syntactic_type|semantic_type. The token that the verbal expression is anchored to is identified by a CTS URN plus token ID.
Example:
#!verbal_units
context|token|syntactic_type|semantic_type
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t3|independent|transitive active


#!tokens
Token analysis blocks begin with a header context|id|tokentype|text|lemma|verbalunit|related1|relationship1|related2|relationship2
Entries in the table token are ordered. Each token is identified by a CTS URN plus token ID, followed by the surface form appearing in the passage and a lemma (headword). The graph structure is recorded by two pairs of fields identifying a token by its ID, and classifying the relationship of the two tokens. In a successful analysis, all non-punctuation tokens have a value for related1 and relationship1; the second pair (related2 and relationship2) have values only for two-way relationships.
Example:
#!tokens
context|id|tokentype|text|lemma|verbalunit|related1|relationship1|related2|relationship2
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t0|lexical|arma|arma||t3|direct object||
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t1|lexical|virum|vir||t3|direct object||
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t2|enclitic|que|que||t0|coordinating conjunction|t1|coordinating conjunction
urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1|t3|lexical|cano|cano|t3|root|unit verb||


#!lm
The optional #!lm block is shaped differently. It has three KEY=value lines per sentence with keys (MODEL, CONTEXT and REASONING. These record the model that produce the anlaysis, the sentences ID as a URN range, and the models reasoning (collapsed to one line).
#!lm
MODEL=litellm_proxy/anthropic/Claude Opus 5
CONTEXT=urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1.t0-urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.omar:1.1.t3
REASONING="arma virumque cano" = "I sing of arms and a man." The only verbal expression is the finite verb "cano" (1st sg. present indicative active), an independent main verb, transitive active, with relatedtoken1 = 'root'. "arma" (neuter accusative plural) and "virum" (accusative singular) are both direct objects of "cano". The enclitic "-que" (here tokenized separately as "que") is a coordinating conjunction joining the two nouns: relatedtoken1 -> "arma", relatedtoken2 -> "virum", both relations 'coordinating conjunction'. Each noun independently keeps its own 'direct object' relation to "cano". No implied tokens are needed; no ambiguity of note ("virum" could theoretically be a genitive plural of "vir", but "arma virumque cano" is unambiguously accusative singular here as a second object of "cano").

title: Allowed values for syntactic relationships
text:
unit verb – the finite verb of a clause, linked either to its subordinating word in subordinate epxressions, or, for independent clauses, to the reserved node value root.
subordinating conjunction – a subordinating word, linked to the verb of the governing clause.
relative pronoun – a relative pronoun, linked both to its antecedent and to its function in the relative clause.
subject – a substantive linked to the verb of its verbal expression.
direct object – a substantive linked to its transitive-active verbal expression.
predicate – a substantive linked to a linking verb.
agent – the head of a prepositional phrase expressing agent with a/ab, linked to a passive verb.
auxiliary – a form of sum linked to a participle in compound forms of the perfect-passive/future-active systems.
object of preposition – a substantive linked to its governing preposition.
adverbial – an adverb, or a prepositional phrase used adverbially, linked to the verb it modifies.
attributive – a prepositional phrase linking to the noun it modifies.
adjectival – an adjective (or gerundive) linking to the noun it agrees with.
genitive – a genitive substantive linked to the noun or verb it modifies.
dative – a dative substantive linked to the noun or verb it relates to.
ablative – an ablative substantive linked to the noun or verb it relates to.
accusative – an accusative substantive that is not the special case of a direct object, linked to the verb or noun it relates to.
vocative – a vocative substantive, linked to the verb of the clause it appears in.
direct quote – verbal expression of directly quoted speech, linked to the verb introducing the direct speech.
aside – verb of a parenthetical aside, linked to the verb of the clause it interrupts.
indirect statement – an infinitive in indirect-statement, linked to the governing verb.
circumstantial participle – a participle linked to the substantive it agrees with.
ablative absolute – an ablative substantive syntactically absolute from the verbal expression where it appears, linked to the verb of the verbal expression.
coordinating conjunction – a coordinating conjunction, linked to the two items (nouns, adjectives, prepositional phrases, or verbal expressions) it joins.
apposition – a substantive in apposition, linked to the subtantive it stands in apposition to.
complementary infinitive – an infinitive completing a governing verb like volo/incipio/audeo/licet/decet, linked to that verb.
praenomen – an abbreviated Roman first-name token, linked to the associated nomen or cognomen.

title: arsgrammatica and the AAT model
text: Agent-Action-Target (AAT) is a universal syntactic model, but it takes a very different approach from the Universal Dependency scheme. Instead of trying to map every syntactic feature of a given language onto a universal scheme, AAT is a reductive model focused on verbal ideas (actions), with their immediate subjects and objects (actors and targets). In Latin, AAT’s actors and targets correspond to subjects and direct objects of transitive active verbs, and to agents and subjects of transitive passive verbs. AAT’s graph maintains coordinated or subordinated ranking of its actions, so it is possible to construct a semantically compatible AAT graph using a subset of the tokens in arsgrammatica’s dependency graph.

title: arsgrammatica and the AAT model
text:
A simple example
Consider a very short Latin sentence, and compare the visualization of the arsgrammatica dependency graphs with its AAT reduction.

arma virumque cano.




arsgrammatica




AAT reduction




The similarity in their structure is obvious. Both graphs take cano for the root; the direct objects of the arsgrammatica graph correspond to the targets of the AAT graph. Note that the AAT reduction, working from the arsgrammatica tokenization where the enclitic -que was correctly handled as a distinct token from virum, omits the conjunction.
Now consider a possible English translation of the same passage. Since the aat package (https://github.com/neelsmith/aat) includes a module implementing the AAT scheme for English, we can juxtapse its AAT graph with the AAT reduction of the Latin passage.

I sing of arms and the man.




AAT graph of translation




AAT graph of Latin




This is a very simple example, but it at least suggests the potential of AAT models for comparing and aligning syntactic structure across languages. We can see that English explicitly names an agent (“I”), where in Latin that role is incorporated in the finite verb form cano; the action and the two targets in each language directly align.

title: Goals of arsgrammatica
text:
Any computational analysis of natural-language syntax must choose a syntactic model suited to its purpose. Some analyses, for example, work with universal syntactic models like Universal Dependencies (UD) or Agent-Action-Target (AAT) to align features across multiple languages.
arsgrammatica addresses a different problem. It defines a syntactic scheme that is unique to Latin in order to support research and teaching focused on Latin texts. Some of its key features include:

title: Goals of arsgrammatica
text:
A simple illustration
Consider a very short Latin sentence, and a diagram of the dependency graph that arsgrammatica builds from it.

arma virumque cano.





Syntactic analysis of a short Latin sentence.



This Latin sentence contains a single verbal expression, rooted in the verb cano. arsgrammatica recognizes four lexical tokens in its dependency graph. It ignores the punctuation token (period), and distinguishes an enclitic token -que from the noun it is orthographically attached to (virum). arsgrammatica identifies two different kinds of relationship in this sentence: direct object and coordinating conjunction.

title: Optimizing with GEPA
text:
One of dspy’s strengths is its streamlined path to optimize a program for a specific configured language model without you having to change any code.


dspy allows you to configure two models: the “teacher” and the “student.”
arsgrammatica configures the target (“student”) model from the same .env file as the rest of arsgrammatica’s programs, with values for API_BASE, MODEL, and API_KEY.
You can configure a more powerful reasoning model to use as the “teacher” by adding a parallel trio of values for REFLECTION_API_BASE, REFLECTION_MODEL, and REFLECTION_API_KEY. GEPA will reason with the “teacher” model while optimizing for the “student” model.
If you do not configure a second reflection model, GEPA will use the same model for both “teacher” and “student.”



The script optimize_gepa.py runs GEPA to improve SentenceAnalysis’s instructions against the gold examples in tests/fixtures/gold_examples.py. This requires making the specified request, and then a further request to a reflection model, so it can potentially be expensive. optimize_gepa lets you regulate this stage of work with these parameters:
python3 optimize_gepa.py                    # --auto light (cheapest; default)
python3 optimize_gepa.py --auto medium       # more thorough, more expensive
python3 optimize_gepa.py --auto heavy        # most thorough, most expensive
python3 optimize_gepa.py --max-metric-calls 40   # exact call budget instead of a preset
python3 optimize_gepa.py --skip-baseline     # skip the pre-GEPA scoring pass (saves N calls)
By default, optimize_gepa trains on all the gold examples in GOLD_EXAMPLES (a small, hand-curated set built to exercise every documented construction at least once) and holds out 20% for an evalution set. The fraction to use as an evaluation set is given in the --val-fraction parameter. You can set it to 0 to use all examples as a training set with no holdout. If you have files of analyses you have verified, you can add those to the testing pool optimize_gepa uses and specify the fraction to be used for an evaluation set:
# Include individual files with analyses:
python3 utilities/optimize_gepa.py --eval-file urn_cts_compnov_bible_genesis_vulgate_42_1.cex urn_cts_compnov_bible_genesis_vulgate_42_2.cex

# Include all files in a directory, and hold out 25% for evaluation set:
python3 utilities/optimize_gepa.py --eval-dir data/vulgate/ --val-fraction 0.25

# Include all files in a directory with no separate evaluation set:
python3 utilities/optimize_gepa.py --eval-dir data/vulgate/ --val-fraction 0 






Tip



The data directory of the arsgrammatica repository includes hand-vetted analyses you can use in optimizing the package for a new model.





arsgrammatica defines a syntax_metric that compares the responses values for verbalunits and tokengraph against the gold answer, and returns a score from 0 to 1. The final metric is computed by weighing a score for correct relations at 50%, a score for classifying verbal expressions at 30%, and scoring for basic fields for each token at 20%. syntax_metric includes specific, human-readable feedback naming every mismatched token/relation/classification, which GEPA’s reflection model can read and take advantage of.



optimize_gepa.py saves the optimized program’s instructions to a JSON file named in the --out parameter or defaulting to optimized_syntax_analysis.json.
To use the saved model, load it right after importing analyze and before calling any analysis functions:
from arsgrammatica.latin_syntax_dspy import analyze
analyze.load("optimized_syntax_analysis.json")






Tip



The optimized directory of the arsgrammatica repository includes saved models in JSON format. File names are based on the target model, the version of arsgrammatica that was targeted, and a directory with the supplementary training data used. A file name like optimized_opus_5_ag_0_7_0_vulgate.json means that this output targeted Opus 5, using arsgrammatica release 0.7.0, with training data from the data/vulgate directory of this repository.

title: Estimating and enforcing a max_tokens budget
text:
SentenceAnalysis’s output (a reasoning field plus JSON-serialized verbalunits/tokengraph) grows with how long and how syntactically complex a sentence is, not by a fixed amount, so a single hard-coded max_tokens value is eventually wrong: too small for a long or deeply subordinated sentence (truncation), too large for a short one (wasted budget). arsgrammatica/token_budget.py addresses this with a calibrate-then-retry approach, and pipeline.py’s analyze_sources() already uses it – both analyze_sources() and analyze_passage() get this for free, with nothing to change in your own calling code.
First, calibrate against your own configured model:
This is a live-LM script (real API cost, one call per GOLD_EXAMPLES entry) that measures how many completion tokens the real model actually uses for each gold example, fits completion_tokens ~= intercept + slope * num_input_tokens by least squares, and writes the result to arsgrammatica/token_budget_calibration.json. Re-run it whenever the configured model, the SentenceAnalysis prompt, or the TokenAnalysis/VerbalExpression schema changes substantially. Until you’ve run it at least once, estimate_max_tokens() falls back to an untuned, deliberately generous placeholder fit – safe, but not a real measurement of your model.
estimate_max_tokens() takes the calibrated (or fallback) fit, multiplies it by a safety_margin (default 1.4, covering reasoning-length variance the fit alone doesn’t), and clamps the result to [floor, ceiling]. Set ceiling to your actual model’s real max-output-tokens limit – the module’s own DEFAULT_CEILING is only a placeholder stand-in, since that limit varies by provider/model and there’s no single correct default.
For the retry half, analyze_with_retry() wraps analyze():
It starts from estimate_max_tokens(len(tokens)) (or initial_max_tokens, if you pass one), and checks the result two ways: whether the returned tokengraph is missing any of tokens’ own ids (the primary, provider-independent signal – a real truncation, LM-JSON getting cut off mid-list, always shows up here), and, as a corroborating check, whether the LM’s own finish_reason was "length". If either signals truncation and a retry is still available (max_retries, default 1) with budget left before ceiling, it multiplies the budget by growth_factor (default 2.0) and calls again – max_tokens is part of DSPy’s own LM cache key, so the retry always reaches the LM again rather than replaying the same truncated cached response. If retries run out: a call that raised re-raises (nothing to fall back to); a call that returned an incomplete result is returned anyway, with a UserWarning naming the missing ids, rather than treated as fatal – consistent with validate()’s own warn-don’t-raise convention for imperfect LM output.
get_calibration() reports which fit is currently active (the real one from calibrate_max_tokens.py, or the untuned fallback) if you want to check before relying on an estimate.

Visualizing syntax graphs with Mermaid
text:
Mermaid is a lightweight diagramming language that is easily used in many Markdown viewers and editors, web environments, the https://mermaid.live mermaid editor, and others. To compose a Mermaid diagram for a token graph:
warnings lists any edge that got skipped because it pointed at a punctuation token or an id missing from tokengraph.

Both tokengraph_to_mermaid and save_mermaid accept one of Mermaid’s orientation codes (BT, TB, LR, RL) in an optional orientation argument, with default value BT (bottom-to-top). Limitations
Mermaid’s layout engine cannot enforce aligning nodes by rank. (You can think of rank as the syntactic depth of the node, like the generations in a family tree.) This kind of alignment can make the diagram of very complex sentences easier to read. If you want diagrams aligned by rank, you can use the open-source graphviz program: see “Diagramming syntactic analyses”.

title: Saving and loading analyses
text: You can serialize analyses to a delimited-text file, and read saved analyses back using the write_analyses and read_analyses functions.

title: Saving and loading analyses
text:
Saving analyses
If you have analyzed one or more passages into two variables sentences and results (like these examples), here’s how to serialize them.
from arsgrammatica import write_analyses, combined_tokengraph

tokengraph = combined_tokengraph(results)
verbalunits = [vu for result in results for vu in result.verbalunits]

warnings = write_analyses(sentences, verbalunits, tokengraph, "analysis.txt")
write_analyses expects sentences, verbal units, and tokens to be separately organized, and writes them to a named file. We already have a sentences variable. We can extract from the results variable separate lists for verbal units (the nested for comprehension) and the token graph (the combined_tokengraph function).
write_analyses returns a list with any warnings encountered in serializing the analyses. We could check those:
for w in warnings:
    print(f"Warning: {w}")
You may also optionally record in a separate block of the delimited-text file the language model and its reasoning as part of the sentence-by-sentence record, using the optional parameters model and reasoning.
import os

warnings = write_analyses(
    sentences, verbalunits, tokengraph, "analysis.txt",
    model=os.environ["MODEL"],
    reasoning=[result.reasoning for result in results],
)

title: Saving and loading analyses
text:
Reading saved analyses
You can read back a flat list of all the four parts of a serialization with the read_analyses function.
from arsgrammatica import read_analyses

tokengraph, verbalunits, sentences, lm_infos = 
    read_analyses("analysis.txt")
To split up the composite token graph by sentence, use split_analysis_by_sentence.
from arsgrammatica import split_analysis_by_sentence
sentencetokens = split_analysis_by_sentence(tokengraph, verbalunits, sentences)

for (sentence_tokengraph, sentence_verbalunits) in 
    zip(sentences, sentencetokens):
    ...  # work with analysis data per sentence
For details of the serialization format, see the reference documentation

title: Tokenizing a source file without full syntax analysis
text:
arsgrammatica ensures that every token in a citable passage is uniquely identified by tokenizing the passage, and assigning identifiers to each token. When you analyze a full passage, arsgrammatica next segments the sequence of tokens into sentence units, and analyzes one sentence at a time.
arsgrammatica’s build-in management of token lengths is very good at preventing the analysis of a single sentence from overflowing your limits on the size of a request and reply. If, however, a single passage contains many long and complex sentences, the total reply from analyzing all the sentences in a passage could still result in a truncated reply. (Anyone interested in reading some orations of Cicero, for example?)
The solution is to submit separate requests for each sentence, but to do that, the tokens must already be uniquely identified. Otherwise the analysis of each sentence would once again begin assigning id values from t0, and tokens would no longer be uniquely identified within their citable context.

title: How to add a gold example
text: A fundamental part of the DSPy development are the GoldExample pairings of a Latin passage with a hand-verified canned_answer. These are defined in tests/fixtures/gold_examples.py. Every GoldExample entry lives in the single GOLD_EXAMPLES list at the bottom of that file. You can add examples there that you have either hand-written, or harvested from successful analyses.

title: How to add a gold example
text:
Harvesting from a successful analysis
If you have analyzed a difficult construction that you want to add to the core training sets, you can save the analysis and use the analysis_to_gold_example.py script to compose the Python you need.
Pass it two arguments: the analysis file, and an identifying label for the analysis. The identifying label is a short, unique, descriptive id (e.g. cicero_proarchia_exordium) that serves as the pytest id for every test parametrized over GOLD_EXAMPLES. Include the --tags parameter to name constructions the example is meant to exercise, for a human skimming the file. Run analysis_to_gold_example -h to see all the optional parameters the script accepts.
Run it like this:
python3 utilities/analysis_to_gold_example.py analysisfile.cex cicero_proarchia_exordium --tags "complex subordination" 
This prints to standard output a string in two parts . The first part is a Python dictionary, which in this example will be named _CICERO_PROARCHIA_EXORDIUM_ANSWER. The dictionary contains the complete analysis data (the model’s reasoning, the verbal expressions table, and the token graph).
The second part is a GoldExample object identifying the labelled analysis as the correct canned_answer for the passage. In our example, it would look like this:

GoldExample(
    slug="cicero_proarchia_exordium",
    passage="ac ne quis a nobis hoc ita dici forte miretur, quod alia quaedam in hoc facultas sit ingeni neque haec dicendi ratio aut disciplina, ne nos quidem huic uni studio penitus umquam dediti fuimus.",
    tags=["complex subordination"],
    canned_answer=_CICERO_PROARCHIA_EXORDIUM_ANSWER,
),
In tests/fixtures/gold_examples.py, you can paste the dict above the list beginning GOLD_EXAMPLES = [ and place the new GoldExample(...) entry inside the list.
Be sure to review the reasoning property of dict you’ve pasted in. It’s the model’s own recorded reasoning, and not guaranteed to read the way you would write it by hand.

title: How to add a gold example
text:
Hand writing a GoldExample
If you want to add a small, deliberately-constructed example targeting one specific construction, refer to the existing examples and:

Write a module-level _SOME_ANSWER = {...} dict: reasoning (a real explanation, not a placeholder), verbalunits (one entry per verbal expression – id/syntactic_type/semantic_type), tokengraph (one entry per token – id/token/tokentype, plus whichever of lemma/verbalunitid/relatedtoken1/relationship1/relatedtoken2/relationship2 actually apply; omit a field entirely rather than setting it to None, matching every existing entry). See arsgrammatica/models.py’s TokenAnalysis/VerbalExpression and syntax_model.md for what’s allowed, and notes/relationship_labels.md for the relation-label catalog.
Add a GoldExample(slug=..., passage=..., tags=[...], canned_answer=_SOME_ANSWER) entry to GOLD_EXAMPLES, referencing that dict.

title: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics
text: Once we have analyzed a passage, we can characterize the resulting syntax graph with standard graph metrics. arsgrammatica includes functions for analyzing graphs in Python, and a Marimo notebook, latin_syntaxer_graphs.py, where you can interactively explore some of these metrics.
crumbs: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics

title: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics
text:
Finding graph metrics
First, from a token graph, we create a graph in the format of the Python NetworkX package:
from arsgrammatica import tokengraph_to_networkx, graph_metrics
nxgraph, warnings = tokengraph_to_networkx(tokengraph)
We can compute graph metrics directly from the NetworkX graph:
metrics = graph_metrics(nxgraph)






Note



Like the diagramming utilities for visualizing graphs in Mermaid or graphviz, arsgrammatica ignores punctuation tokens in these metrics.


The resulting variable metrics has a number of properties that can help us understand the size, complexity, and “shape” of the syntax analysis’ graph structure.
crumbs: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics

title: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics
text:
Size
node_count and edge_count properties tell us the number of tokens and the number of relations connecting tokens in our syntax graph. If the graph is not cyclic, longest_chain tells us the deepest level of token relations in the sentence. longest_chain is None when a a graph includes a cycle.
If we analyzed an artificial sentence like Rosa pulchra est, we could visualize the graph like this:



Toy example of a syntax graph.


It has a node count of 3, edge count of 2, and a longest chain of 1.
crumbs: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics

title: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics
text:
“Shape” (topology)
leaf_count tells you the number of tokens that no other tokens depend on (the “leaves” in a tree visiualization). leaf_fraction gives you the proportion of nodes in the graph that are leaf nodes. In the toy example, two nodes are leaf nodes (Rosa and pulchra), and the leaf fraction is 67% (2/3).
The example syntax graph is a tree: every node is connected and there are no cycles or loops in the graph. Most syntax graphs come close to a tree structure, but tokens like relative pronouns (that are related both to their antecedent and to their function in the relative clause) can create cycles. The cyclomatic_number gives a measure of “how much non-tree structure does this sentence have?” (More techncially, it gives the number edges beyond a spanning tree, computed as edge_count - node_count + weakly_connected_components). The cyclomatic number in the example is 0, because the entire graph is a true tree.
crumbs: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics

title: Characterizing syntax analyses with graph metrics
text:
Organization of the graph
arsgrammatica’s syntax graphs are directed: pairs of nodes are connected from one node to another (e.g., the subject relationship makes a connection from a subject to its verb). For any node, the in-degree is the number of relations point to it, and the out-degree is the number of relations it points out to. In the example above, est has an in-degree of 2, and an out-degree of 0.
The mean_dependents and max_dependents measure the average and maximum in-degree of the graph. If a sentence has a high maximum compare to its node count, that tells us one token controls most of the syntax. Lower values with mean and maximum closer to each other suggests a “shallow and bushy” structure rather than a “deep and chainy” organization.

title: Comparing models with model_bakeoff.py
text:
arsgrammatica was developed with Claude Opus 5 hosted at the College of the Holy Cross. dspy lets us plug in other models and use the same code with them. What open-weight models hosted on Hugging Face, or running locally under Ollama could realistically run arsgrammatica?
model_bakeoff.py lets you compare multiple models against the same held-out slice of gold examples, and see not just whether each one is “good enough” but where it falls short and whether that performance can be improved. You can run model_bakeoff.py whenever you want to evaluate a candidate; it never affects the production pipeline.


“Can a given model run arsgrammatica?” is really three separate questions:

How good is the model with the instructions already written and tuned against Opus 5, without optimization?
How much does the performance improve if we let dspy.GEPA optimize instructions for the model?
How much does the performance improve if we use Opus 5 as a “teacher” model and modify the candidate model’s instructions?

You can answer each of those questions with the model_bakeoff.py script, selecting from these values for the --stages:

baseline : zero-shot testing answering question 1, how good is the model without optimization? The cheapest stage by far (one call per held-out example) and worth running alone first.
gepa — uses dspy.GEPA to rewrite the instructions for the candidate model. The candidate still solves every example itself, both during optimization and at final scoring; only the wording changes. This answers question 2.
bootstrap uses Opus 5 as a “teacher” model, and attaches verified correct traces to the model’s instructions as few-shot examples. Here the candidate never has to solve a training example itself — only the held-out scoring examples afterward.

title: Improving arsgrammatica by reading Latin
text:
You can incorporate the results of reading real Latin texts with arsgrammatica into a repeatable development loop that constantly improves the package.


When arsgrammatica fails to analyze the syntax of a passage correctly, we can use the results to identify gaps in the schema, or areas in need of better training.
First check whether syntax_model.md explicitly and clearly defines the construction that was not analyzed correctly. If it does not, modify syntax_model.md and follow the steps given in the reference section to extend the scheme for the new construction.
If the scheme is already clear, but the analysis failed anyway, use this recipe to add a GoldExample with a correct canned_answer in tests/fixtures/gold_examples.py. If you’re unsure between two defensible readings, say so explicitly in a comment above the fixture rather than silently committing to one.
Re-run pytest to confirm that the new or corrected fixture validates and that test_coverage.py is satisfied.



When arsgrammatica correctly analyzes a passage, that is real evidence that the model is working correctly. We can save manually vetted examples as checks to ensure that future changes to a prompt or model can’t silently break this case, and to extend the evaluation pool for later optimization.


If the response correctly analyzes an unusual or difficult construction that you think it might not always get right, this is worth reinforcing in the core training set. If you save the analysis to a file, you can use the script utilities/analysis_to_gold_example.py to write the necessary Python for you that you can paste in to gold_examples.py.



If the analysis correctly identified something you already expected it to get right, such as a simple independent clause with direct object, this is still real evidence, but of low value as training signal. If we add more examples of easy cases that the model already gets right, it teaches the optimizer nothing new, and dilutes the training set with redundant coverage.
Instead, serialize and save the analysis in a directory you can later pass to optimize_gepa.py with the --eval-dir parameter as part of the larger training and evaluation set.




Every addition to GOLD_EXAMPLES (whether a correction for a failure or a harvested success with a rare construction) becomes part of the training set for the next time optimize_gepa.py runs.
Every analysis you save expands the pool GEPA can use to optimize prompts for specific models.



If you save a large number of correct analyses as you work through a corpus, and then include all those analyses in the training set for GEPA, the result might perform better on your particular corpus, but worse on a broader corpus of Latin. In one experiment, for example, an optimized model drawing on a large number of analyzed passages from the Latin Vulgate performed worse on a selection of passages from Livy than an unoptimized generic model. Presumably it would do better on further passages of the Vulgate.
Your specific strategy for optimization will depend on your goal: do want a more specialized system tailored to a particular corpus, or a more generally applicable system?






Note



The github repository for arsgrammatica organizes a selection of hand-vetted analyses in subdirectories of the data directory by corpus, so they can easily be included or excluded with the --eval-dir parameter to optimize_gepa.py.

title: arsgrammatica and Universal Dependencies
text:
The Universal Dependencies framework (UD) proposes annotation schemes for parts of speech, morphological features, and syntactic dependencies to apply across many languages, that have already been applied to more than 150 languages. UD is especially significant to Latinists because of Patrick Burns’ work on LatinCy, language models that work with the Python spaCy package for natural-language processing. Each token analyzed with spaCy has a head property linking it to another token in the syntax graph, and a dep_ property with the UD annotation for syntactic relationship (dependency).






TipThe udsyntax package



spaCy’s annotations for each analyzed token are extensive, but include many elements that are not helpful for Latinists (e.g., like_email, like_url). You can extract the syntactic relations from spaCy’s tokens into a simple syntactic graph structure with the udsyntax package.

title: arsgrammatica and Universal Dependencies
text:
A simple illustration
Consider a very short Latin sentence, and a visualization of the dependency graphs that UD annotation and arsgrammatica build for it.

arma virumque cano.








UD
arsgrammatica













Several features of the UD graph will seem odd to a Latinist. The UD has only one direct object (tagged obj) of the verb token cano. The noun uirum is tagged as a dependency of arma, in the relation tagged conj. The conjunction que is not related to virum but is a dependency of arma. The terminal period appears as part of the syntactic analysis.
arsgrammatica’s Latin-focused graph is a more natural representation for research questions like “What are the direct objects in this sentence?” In Latin classrooms, many teachers may find the UD representation unusuable or simply “wrong.” arsgrammatica’s representation more closely follows what students will find in Latin textbooks.

title: arsgrammatica and Universal Dependencies
text:
Two graph-theoretic details

The UD guidelines guarantee that all syntax graphs are trees. As this example shows, that is not true for arsgrammatica’s directed graphs. In fact, although arsgrammatica’s syntax graphs often approximate a tree structure, they are not guaranteed to be acyclic either: elements like relative pronouns have relations both to their antecedent and to their function in the relative clause, which can set up cycles. (See examples with relative pronouns in the documentation.)
UD graphs are oriented with relations from root-level verbal structures flowing down; arsgrammatica graphs are oriented so that related elements from up to root-level verbal structures.

AAT relations
The Agent-Action-Target model focuses on two special relations to verbal expressions: the agent and the target. In Latin (as in English), these relations are constructed differently depending on the voice of the verbal expression. Agency is expressed by the subject of transitive active, intransitive, and linking verbs, and by the ablative of agent construction with passive verbs. Target status is expressed by the direct object of transitive active verbs, the predicate of linking verbs, and by the subject of transitive passive verbs.

title: A command-line script for analyzing Latin syntax
text:
syntaxer_main.py reads authentication credentials for your LM from your environment and analyzes a passage. It writes the result in to standard output in arsgrammatica’s standard serialization format. Create an .env to configure your LM credentials, like this:
API_BASE=https://localmodel/api
MODEL=litellm/modelname
API_KEY=your-key-here
Then run syntaxer_main.py with a passage argument:
python3 syntaxer_main.py --passage "Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres."
To include a citation reference (e.g. a CTS URN), use the --citation argument:
python3 syntaxer_main.py --passage "Arma virumque canō." --citation "urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.perseus:1.1"
Redirect the output to a file with standard IO redirection:
python3 syntaxer_main.py --passage "Arma virumque canō." 
    --citation "urn:cts:latinLit:phi0690.phi003.perseus:1.1" > aeneid_analysis.cex

title: Running tests with pytest
text:
Off-line testing
The whole pytest suite runs against DummyLM, not a real model. In tests/fixtures/gold_examples.py’s, GOLD_EXAMPLES defines a deliberately curated corpus. test_coverage.py enforces that every documented relation label, verbal-expression classification, and token type has at least one example exercising it.
Tests that call the configured LM are marked live and skipped by default. To run all offline tests:
pytest

text:
Testing with a real model
Testing uses the model configured in your .env file. Run the live tests:
pytest -m live

title: How arsgrammatica keeps the token size manageable
text: When arsgrammatica submits a passage to analyze to a configured language model, the prompt it submits includes a lengthy specification of how to analyze Latin syntax in the specific scheme used in this package. The reply from the LM includes a token-by-token analysis that will vary in length depending on the length of the passage submitted. The inevitable result is that each analysis requires a very large context: Latin syntax is complicated. arsgrammatica includes a couple of tricks to help manage that.
crumbs: How `arsgrammatica` keeps the token size manageable

title: How arsgrammatica keeps the token size manageable
section: Work one sentence at a time, not a whole passage at once
text:
Work one sentence at a time, not a whole passage at once
The most basic way this package keeps requests manageable is by breaking passages into individual sentences, then analyzing each sentence separately, one request at a time.
crumbs: How `arsgrammatica` keeps the token size manageable

title: How arsgrammatica keeps the token size manageable
section: Make an educated guess about how much room the answer will need
text:
Make an educated guess about how much room the answer will need
For each analysis request, the package sends a maximum size for the complete context. If the figure is too low, long replies are truncated. If it too is high, and you’re routinely paying for (and waiting on) more headroom than any answer actually uses, and you risk exceeding hardcoded limits to the model you’re using.
The package includes an optional “calibration” step to estimate how long a give LM’s answers tend to be for sentences of a given length. It estimates a figure for maximum context size tht is roughly in proportion to how long the sentence is, plus fixed overhead for the static instructions, plus some extra padding since a sentence’s syntactic complexity isn’t predictable just from its length; two sentences of the same length can still need noticeably different amounts of explanation. Once you have calibrated a given model, the package can look at a new sentence’s length and make an informed guess about how much room to leave for its answer.
To take advantage of this feature, run python3 calibrate_max_tokens.py. (This can be slow because it runs through all the examples in the “gold” training set.)
If nobody has ever run that calibration step yet – say, the first time the package is used against a new model – arsgrammatica falls back to a deliberately generous, cautious estimate that’s designed to err on the side of leaving too much room rather than too little, until a real calibration can replace it with something more precisely tuned.
crumbs: How `arsgrammatica` keeps the token size manageable

title: How arsgrammatica keeps the token size manageable
section: Check the answer, and ask again if it came back cut short
text:
Check the answer, and ask again if it came back cut short
arsgrammatica checks responses from the LM to see if the reply is complete. The most reliable check is simple: does the returned analysis account for every single word of the original sentence? If a word is unaccounted for, the answer was probably cut off partway through. As a second, corroborating check, the package also looks at whether the LM provider itself flagged the response as having been stopped early for running out of room.
When either check suggests the answer was cut short, the package resubmits the same sentence, but with meaningfully more writing room allowed this time, and again checks the new response the same way. It’s willing to try this a couple of times, giving the LM progressively more room on each attempt, before it stops.
If, after those extra attempts, the answer still looks incomplete, arsgrammatica returns the best answer it has, but flags it clearly with a warning naming exactly what appears to be missing.
crumbs: How `arsgrammatica` keeps the token size manageable

title: How arsgrammatica keeps the token size manageable
section: Reusing the instructions instead of resending them every time
text:
Reusing the instructions instead of resending them every time
arsgrammatica also takes advantage of a feature some AI providers offer, sometimes called “prompt caching.” This lets the provider remember the lengthy, unchanging block of instructions from one request to the next. Since this is the longest part of a prompt-request exchange, that meaningfully cuts down the real-world cost and time of running multiple sentences through the package.
crumbs: How `arsgrammatica` keeps the token size manageable
